text: The 2010 FIFA World Cup was the 19th edition of the world championship for men's national football teams, held in South Africa from 11 June to 11 July 2010. The bidding process was open only to African nations, with five countries submitting bids: Egypt, Morocco, South Africa, and a joint bid from Libya and Tunisia. Following a vote in May 2004, South Africa was selected over Egypt and Morocco to become the first African nation to host the finals; the decision was announced by FIFA president Sepp Blatter in Zürich, with South Africa receiving 14 votes, Morocco 10, and Egypt zero. The tournament took place in 10 stadiums across nine host cities, with the opening and final held at Soccer City in Johannesburg. Thirty-two teams qualified through a worldwide qualification tournament that began in August 2007, with the host nation South Africa qualifying automatically. The teams were divided into eight groups of four for the group stage, where the top two teams from each group advanced to the knockout stage, which consisted of four rounds—round of 16, quarter-finals, semi-finals, and final—followed by a play-off for third and fourth place. In the final, Spain defeated the Netherlands 1–0 after extra time to win their first World Cup title, becoming the eighth nation to win the tournament and the first European team to win a World Cup hosted outside Europe. Spain also became the first national team to win the tournament after losing their first match and the first team since 1978 to win a World Cup after losing a group stage match. As a result, Spain represented the world at the 2013 FIFA Confederations Cup. South Africa, the host nation, was eliminated in the group stage, as were the 2006 finalists Italy and France, marking the first time hosts had been eliminated in the group stage and the first of three consecutive World Cups in which the defending champions were eliminated in the group stage. New Zealand, with three draws, were the only undefeated team but also eliminated in the group stage. The qualification draw was held in Durban on 25 November 2007, and the tournament featured 204 of the 208 FIFA national teams, sharing the record for most competing nations with the 2008 Summer Olympics. Teams that failed to qualify included Saudi Arabia, Tunisia, Croatia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Poland, Sweden, Ukraine, Russia, and Turkey. The highest-ranked team not to qualify was Croatia (ranked 10th), while the lowest-ranked team that qualified was North Korea (ranked 105th). As of 2025, this was the last time North Korea, Slovakia, and Slovenia qualified for a FIFA World Cup finals, and the last time Belgium, Iran, and Croatia failed to qualify. Five new stadiums were built and five existing venues upgraded, with construction costs estimated at R8.4 billion (just over US$1 billion or €950 million). Public transport infrastructure, including Johannesburg's Gautrain and other metro systems, was improved. Special safety measures were implemented, including temporary flight restrictions around stadiums. On 8 July 2009, 70,000 construction workers walked off their jobs due to allegations of underpayment, but the strike was resolved within a week, and all stadiums were completed on time. The total prize money was US$420 million, a 60 percent increase from 2006, including US$40 million paid to domestic clubs—a first for the World Cup due to an agreement between FIFA and European clubs to settle claims from past injuries. The 2010 World Cup used 12 provisional venues, narrowed to ten officially announced by FIFA on 17 March 2006. Six of the ten venues were over 1,200 meters above sea level, with the two Johannesburg stadiums—FNB Stadium (Soccer City) and Ellis Park Stadium—at approximately 1,750 meters. FNB Stadium, Cape Town Stadium, and Nelson Mandela Bay Stadium each hosted eight matches, while Ellis Park and Moses Mabhida hosted seven each, and Loftus Versfeld, Free State, and Royal Bafokeng hosted six each. Peter Mokaba and Mbombela hosted four matches each but no knockout-stage matches. The group draw was held in Cape Town on 4 December 2009, presented by Charlize Theron and Jérôme Valcke, with balls drawn by David Beckham, Haile Gebrselassie, John Smit, Makhaya Ntini, Matthew Booth, and Simphiwe Dludlu. FIFA selected 29 referees, including four from AFC, three from CAF, six from CONMEBOL, four from CONCACAF, two from OFC, and ten from UEFA. English referee Howard Webb officiated the final, becoming the first person to referee both the UEFA Champions League final and the World Cup final in the same year. Each team fielded 23 players, with final squads confirmed by 1 June 2010 and late replacements allowed for serious injuries up to 24 hours before a match. Of the 736 players, over half played in European leagues, primarily in England (117), Germany (84), Italy (80), Spain (59), and France (46). The English, German, and Italian squads consisted entirely of home-based players, while only Nigeria had no players from clubs in their own league. FC Barcelona contributed the most players (13), with seven other clubs contributing 10 or more. Honduras's squad included three siblings—Jerry, Johnny, and Wilson Palacios—marking a first for the tournament, and Germany and Ghana had two brothers playing for opposing nations, Jérôme Boateng and Kevin-Prince Boateng. The 32 teams played 64 matches, progressing through the group stage and knockout rounds, with rest days allocated for player recovery. Preliminary events were held to celebrate the tournament. All match times were in South African Standard Time (UTC+2). The South American teams performed strongly, with all five advancing to the round of 16 (four as group winners) and four reaching the quarter-finals, though only Uruguay advanced to the semi-finals. Of the six African teams, only Ghana advanced to the round of 16, and South Africa became the first host nation to be eliminated in the group stage despite beating France and drawing with Mexico. Ghana and Ivory Coast were the only African teams to win a match, and the overall African performance was considered disappointing by observers like Roger Milla. Only six of the 13 UEFA teams advanced to the round of 16, a record low since 1986, but the final was contested by two European teams. Italy and France, the 2006 finalists, were both eliminated in the group stage, with Italy becoming the third defending champion to be eliminated in the first round after Brazil in 1966 and France in 2002. New Zealand, despite being one of the lowest-ranked teams, drew all three of their group matches and ended the tournament as the only undefeated team. In a controversial incident, FIFA President Sepp Blatter apologized to England and Mexico for refereeing errors.

New Zealand, one of the lowest-ranked teams, surprised many by drawing all three of their group matches and ending the tournament as the only undefeated team. The knockout stage featured 16 teams advancing from the group stage, consisting of four rounds—round of 16, quarter-finals, semi-finals, and the final—with each round eliminating half the teams. Any draw at 90 minutes was followed by 30 minutes of extra time, and if the scores remained level, a penalty shoot-out determined progression. In the round of 16, each group winner (A to H) was paired against the runner-up from another group. The round was marked by controversial refereeing decisions, prompting FIFA President Sepp Blatter to apologize to England and Mexico for the errors, stating that "you can win some and you lose some," and promising to re-open discussions on goal-line technology and video replays, with the first opportunity to discuss it occurring at the July business meeting. The three quarter-finals between European and South American teams all ended in European victories: Germany defeated Argentina 4–0, the Netherlands came from behind to beat Brazil 2–1 (marking Brazil’s first loss in a World Cup match outside Europe since 1950), and Spain won 1–0 over Paraguay to reach the final for the first time since 1950. Uruguay, the only South American team to reach the semi-finals, advanced after a 1–1 draw with Ghana, which missed a penalty in extra time following Luis Suárez’s handball on the line. The Netherlands qualified for the final for the third time with a 3–2 win over Uruguay, and Spain reached their first final with a 1–0 victory over Germany, making it the first World Cup final without Brazil, Italy, Germany, or Argentina, and ensuring a new champion as neither Spain nor the Netherlands had previously won the tournament. Germany defeated Uruguay 3–2 to secure third place, holding the record for most third-place finishes (4), while Uruguay holds the record for most fourth-place finishes (3). The final was held on 11 July 2010 at Soccer City, Johannesburg, where Spain defeated the Netherlands 1–0 in extra time, with Andrés Iniesta scoring the goal in the 116th minute—the latest winning goal in a FIFA World Cup final. This victory gave Spain their first World Cup title, making them the eighth team to win it, the first new winner without home advantage since Brazil in 1958, and the first team to win after losing their opening match. The final saw 14 yellow cards, more than doubling the previous record set in 1986, and John Heitinga was sent off for a second yellow card. The Netherlands had a key chance in the 60th minute when Arjen Robben was released by Wesley Sneijder to face Iker Casillas, who saved the shot. Iniesta broke the deadlock with a volleyed shot from a pass by Cesc Fàbregas. This result marked the first time two teams from the same continent won consecutive World Cups (after Italy in 2006), and Europe reached 10 titles, surpassing South America’s nine. Spain became the first European nation to win a World Cup not hosted on European soil and the first team since West Germany in 1974 to win as European champions. Spain also set a record for the fewest goals scored by a World Cup-winning team (eight), the fewest goalscorers (three: Villa with five, Iniesta with two, Puyol with one), and the fewest goals conceded (two, equaling Italy in 2006 and France in 1998), and became the first team to win the World Cup without conceding a goal in the knockout stage. The four top scorers in the tournament each scored five goals, all from teams finishing in the top four—Spain, the Netherlands, Germany, and Uruguay. The Golden Boot went to Thomas Müller of Germany (three assists), the Silver Boot to David Villa of Spain (635 minutes), and the Bronze Boot to Wesley Sneijder of the Netherlands (652 minutes); Diego Forlán of Uruguay scored five goals and one assist in 654 minutes, and three other players scored four goals. Only 145 goals were scored at the 2010 World Cup, the lowest in any FIFA World Cup since the 64-game format began, following 171 in 1998, 161 in 2002, and 147 in 2006. Twenty-eight players were suspended for two yellow cards (13), one red card (8), or a yellow followed by a red (7). FIFA released a final ranking based on progress, results, and quality of opposition, and an All-Star Team based on the Castrol performance index. The Dream Team, selected by public vote until 11 July 2010, included six players from Spain (including the coach), two from Germany, and one each from Brazil, the Netherlands, and Uruguay. The 2010 World Cup amplified public awareness of the vuvuzela, a long horn blown by fans, with complaints from players like Patrice Evra, Lionel Messi, and broadcasters about the noise disrupting communication and commentary. Some viewers reported that the ambient audio feed contained only vuvuzela sounds. ESPN and the BBC explored options for noise-free broadcasts. The official mascot was Zakumi, an African leopard with green hair, named from "ZA" and "kumi" (ten), reflecting South Africa’s colors of yellow and green. The match ball, Jabulani, manufactured by Adidas, meant "bringing joy to everyone," featured 11 colors representing each player and the 11 official languages of South Africa, and used eight thermally bonded, three-dimensional panels made from EVA and TPU with a GripnGroove textured surface developed in partnership with Loughborough University. The ball was made in China, with latex bladders from India, TPU from Taiwan, and other materials from China. Some players criticized the ball’s unpredictable movement, with Júlio César calling it a "supermarket" ball and Maradona stating long passes were unlikely, though some Adidas-sponsored players praised it. The official song, "Waka Waka (This Time for Africa)," performed by Shakira and Freshlyground, was based on the traditional African song "Zangalewa" and performed at the pre-tournament concert, opening, and closing ceremonies. The official mascot song was "Game On," and the anthem was "Sign of a Victory" by R. Kelly with the Soweto Spiritual Singers, performed at the opening ceremony. Danny Jordaan dismissed concerns that the attack on the Togo team in Angola in January 2010 affected security, though reports of thefts against tourists from China, Portugal, Spain, South Korea, Japan, and Colombia emerged. After the England vs. Algeria match on 19 June, a fan broke into the England dressing room shortly after Prince William and Prince Harry left, was released before police intervention, and the Football Association filed a formal complaint with FIFA demanding improved security. The tournament was linked to evictions, with the Abahlali baseMjondolo movement taking the KwaZulu-Natal government to court over the Elimination and Prevention of Re-Emergence of Slums Act, and the N2 Gateway project in Cape Town planning to remove over 20,000 residents from Joe Slovo Informal Settlement to build rental flats. NGOs and human rights groups criticized the conditions in Blikkiesdorp and accused the project of displacing poor families. Some argued that evictions were common in South Africa and that many were wrongly attributed to the World Cup. FIFA’s media control led to legal disputes with an international rugby match, a South African airline, and TV networks. Group ticket holders who did not use all their tickets led to early-round matches with up to 11,000 unoccupied seats. While the event boosted South Africa’s image, it was a major financial disappointment: construction costs totaled £3 billion (€3.6 billion), with expected tourism revenue of £570 million (€680 million), but only £323 million (€385 million) was generated from 309,000 foreign visitors, far below the expected 450,000. Local vendors were banned from selling food and merchandise within 1.5 kilometers of stadiums, requiring a R60,000 registration fee—unaffordable for most—limiting access to local South African food and culture. FIFA President Sepp Blatter declared the event a "huge financial success" for Africa, South Africa, and FIFA, citing revenue of £2.24 billion (€2 billion), and in a December 2010 Quality Progress, rated South Africa’s organization a nine out of ten, citing a lack of public transportation as the main issue. The 2010 FIFA World Cup was expected to be the most-watched television event in history, with hundreds of broadcasters from about 70 countries reaching a cumulative audience of over 26 billion people, averaging approximately 400 million viewers per match, and around 700 million expected to watch the final. New digital media allowed live coverage through alternative platforms.

FIFA President Sepp Blatter declared the 2010 FIFA World Cup "a huge financial success for everybody, for Africa, for South Africa and for FIFA," with revenue to FIFA amounting to £2.24 billion (€2 billion). In a December 2010 article in Quality Progress, Blatter rated South Africa's organisational efforts a nine out of 10, stating that South Africa could serve as a plan B for all future competitions, with the South African Quality Institute (SAQI) assisting in facility construction, event promotion, and organisation; the main issue identified was a lack of sufficient public transportation. The 2010 FIFA World Cup was expected to be the most-watched television event in history, with hundreds of broadcasters from about 70 countries transmitting the event to a cumulative TV audience that FIFA officials estimated would exceed 26 billion people, averaging approximately 400 million viewers per match, and around 700 million viewers expected to watch the final. New digital media allowed viewers to access coverage via cell phones and computers, with Jake Coyle of the Associated Press stating that the World Cup would receive more online coverage than any major sporting event. In the United States, ABC, ESPN, and ESPN2 averaged a 2.1 rating, reaching 2,288,000 households and 3,261,000 viewers for the 64 matches, a 31 percent increase in rating from 2006's 1.6, with households rising 32 percent from 1,735,000 and viewers increasing from 2,316,000; during the first 50 games, the rating increased by 48 percent, households by 54 percent, and viewers by 60 percent. Univision averaged 2,624,000 viewers, up 17 percent, and 1,625,000 households, an 11 percent increase. A Nielsen Company executive described the viewership for the U.S. versus Ghana match as "phenomenal." Live streaming on ESPN3.com attracted some of the largest audiences in history, with 7.4 million unique viewers tuning in, generating 942 million minutes of viewing—over two hours per unique viewer—and all 64 live matches averaging 114,000 viewers per minute; the semi-final between Spain and Germany reached 355,000 viewers per minute, the highest average on ESPN3.com. Sony technology was used to film the tournament, with 25 matches captured using 3D cameras via Sony's proprietary multi-image MPE-200 processors in specially designed 3D outside broadcast trucks, employing its flagship HDC-1500 cameras and new HDC-P1 unit, a compact point-of-view camera with 3, 2/3-inch CCD sensors; the 3D games were produced for FIFA by Host Broadcast Services. In PlayStation Home, Sony released a virtual space based on the 2010 FIFA World Cup in the Japanese version on 3 December 2009, called "FevaArena," a virtual stadium featuring event areas, a FIFA mini-game, and a shop with FIFA-related content. On 27 April 2010, EA Sports released the official 2010 World Cup video game. FIFA expanded the FIFA Fan Fest, hosting events in Sydney, Buenos Aires, Berlin, Paris, Rome, Rio de Janeiro, Mexico City, and several venues around South Africa, with the Durban Fan Fest being the most popular in South Africa, followed by the Cape Town Fan Fest.
